title: How much is it?
goal: Master the famously strange Danish number system, give and ask for prices, and read phone numbers and dates.
bekal: count to a thousand, including 50–90, which are built on multiples of twenty
wave: Go back over **Unit 4** first: take ten nouns and say all four forms in a row — *en bil, bilen, biler, bilerne*.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — På loppemarkedet
dialogs.intro: A Sunday flea market at Israels Plads. Budi haggles over a secondhand bike.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Excuse me, how much is the bike?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Otte hundrede? Det er lidt dyrt.
lines.id: Eight hundred? That's a bit expensive.
lines.literal: eight hundred? it is little expensive.

lines.speaker: Sælger:
lines.text: Den er kun to år gammel. Se på bremserne.
lines.id: It's only two years old. Look at the brakes.
lines.literal: it is only two years old. look at brakes-the.

lines.speaker: Sælger:
lines.text: Syvhundrede og halvtreds. Så er der en lås med.
lines.id: Seven hundred and fifty. The lock's included.
lines.literal: seven-hundred and fifty. then is there a lock with.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Seven hundred. I only have cash.

lines.speaker: Sælger:
lines.text: Okay, det er en aftale. Syvhundrede.
lines.id: Okay, it's a deal. Seven hundred.
lines.literal: okay, it is a deal. seven-hundred.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Here you are. Seven hundred-kroner notes.

lines.speaker: Sælger:
lines.text: Perfekt. Og her er nøglen til låsen.
lines.id: Perfect. And here's the key to the lock.
lines.literal: perfect. and here is key-the to lock-the.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tusind tak. Hav en god dag!
lines.id: Thanks so much. Have a nice day!
lines.literal: thousand thanks. have a good day!

notes: **Hvad koster det?** is the most common way to ask a price. There's also *Hvor meget koster det?* — same meaning, a bit longer.

**Kroner, not krone.** The Danish currency is *en krone* (plural *kroner*), shortened to **kr.** or **DKK**. A hundred *øre* make one krone, but øre coins went out of use long ago; prices are always rounded.
**Kun** = "only". Don't confuse it with *kan* (can). Two short words that sound close but mean very different things.
**Så** has many jobs: "then", "so", "in that case", and as an intensifier (*så dyrt!* = so expensive!). It's one of the most frequent words in Danish conversation.

**Kontanter** = cash, always plural. Worth knowing: Denmark is almost entirely cashless. Outside flea markets, you'll pay for almost everything with a *Dankort* or *MobilePay*. The sentence you'll need more often is *Kan jeg betale med kort?*
**Hav en god dag** — the command form of *at have* is *hav*. This phrase is fairly new in Danish, borrowed from English "have a nice day", but it's now common in shops.
**Hundredekronesedler** — a three-level compound: *hundrede* + *krone* + *sedler* (banknotes). If you can take it apart, you've mastered the way to read written Danish.

grammars.title: Numbers 20–100: the system that makes people give up
body: This is the most famously strange part of Danish, and its reputation is well earned. Norwegian and Swedish build 50–90 from multiples of **ten**, like almost every language in the world. Danish kept an ancient way of counting based on **twenty**.
The good news: you only need to memorize five words. The logic behind them can be ignored completely — even Danes don't think about it.
after: The last column is just to satisfy your curiosity. "Half-third" means two and a half — a way of counting that also existed in old German. English has a cousin of the idea in "score" (*four score and seven years*). Don't memorize that column; memorize the second one.
⚠️ There are longer official forms for checks and financial documents: *halvtredsindstyve*, *tresindstyve*, and so on. You'll never say them, but you might read them.

grammars.title: The ones come first
body: After 20, Danish says **the ones first, then the tens**, joined with *og* (and) — like the old English nursery rhyme "four-and-twenty blackbirds". If you've studied German or Dutch, you know this pattern. If not, it takes real practice.
after: Everything up to 99 is written **as one word with no spaces**: *seksoghalvfjerds*. From the hundreds on, the parts are written separately, with *og* before the tens.

What takes the most effort at first isn't saying them but **hearing** them. When the cashier says *toogfirs*, your brain hears "two" first and has already guessed something in the twenties. The fix: listen all the way to the end before translating.
An emergency trick at the checkout: almost every Danish till has a display showing the amount. There's no harm in glancing at it while you learn.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *For* in front of an adjective means "too", not "for": *for dyrt* = too expensive, *for lille* = too small. A short word whose meaning changes completely depending on where it stands.

Note *Har **I** noget billigere?* — capital *I*, meaning "you (plural)". In a shop, Danes address the staff as "you all" on behalf of the store, much as English speakers ask "Do you have…?" meaning the shop, not the person.
Danish phone numbers always have eight digits, and they're read out **in pairs** — which means all the number weirdness above gets used right away.
Dates use ordinal numbers, formed by adding **-ende** or **-te**. The first eleven are irregular and must be memorized:

head: Dansk
English
rows: Jeg har fødselsdag den syttende august.
My birthday is on the seventeenth of August.

blocks.title: Number practice that really works
items: Read your own phone number out loud in Danish once a day. Eight digits, four pairs — and almost certainly at least one number between 50 and 90.
Every time you see a price anywhere today, say it silently in Danish. The prices around you are an endless, free source of practice.
Numbers are the one part of a language that has to be **automatic**. If you're still calculating in your head when you hear *halvfjerds*, you've already missed the next three sentences.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: fireogtyve — otteogtredive — enoghalvtreds — syvogtres — tooghalvfjerds — niogfirs — femoghalvfems — hundrede og halvtreds
Hvad koster cyklen? — Den koster syv hundrede kroner. — Det er for dyrt. — Kan jeg betale med kort? — Har I noget billigere? — Jeg tager den.
Hvad koster det? — Den koster halvfjerds kroner. — Det er for dyrt. — Kan jeg betale med kort? — Jeg tager den.
